posts.blog_title: EU AI Act: What Every Recruiting Agency Must Know About AI Compliance
posts.text:
The EU AI Act doesn't just apply to companies building AI.

It applies to recruiting agencies that USE it.

If you run CV screening, candidate ranking, or automated scoring through an ATS — your agency is classified as a "deployer" under the regulation. And deployers have real legal obligations starting August 2026.

This surprised a lot of agency owners I've spoken to recently. They assumed compliance was someone else's problem — the AI vendor's job.

It's not.

As the deployer, you're responsible for:
— Informing candidates that AI played a role in decisions about them
— Keeping a human in the loop who can override AI outputs
— Logging how and when your high-risk AI systems are used
— Ensuring candidates can request a human review

The good news: most of this is process, not technology. You don't need to rip out your ATS or stop using AI tools. You need to document what you do and be transparent about it.

The agencies that get ahead of this now won't be scrambling in 2026 — and they'll have a real differentiator with clients who ask about AI governance.

What's the one AI tool in your recruiting workflow you've never thought of as "regulated"?

posts.blog_title: EU AI Act: What Every Recruiting Agency Must Know About AI Compliance
posts.text:
Your 7-step EU AI Act compliance checklist for recruiting agencies.

August 2026 is the hard deadline for deployers of high-risk AI. That's sooner than it sounds once you factor in updating contracts, rewriting candidate comms, and training your team.

Here's where to start today:

1. Inventory every AI tool you use — ATS ranking features, CV screeners, video interview analysis, outreach automation. All of it.

2. Classify each tool by risk tier. Does it score, filter, or rank candidates? High-risk. Does it only communicate or schedule? Limited risk.

3. Ask your vendors where they stand on compliance. High-risk AI providers have their own obligations — conformity assessments, CE marking from August 2026. If they can't answer, that's a red flag.

4. Update your candidate disclosures. Add AI transparency language to application forms, privacy notices, and automated emails. One clear sentence is enough.

5. Document your human oversight process. Who reviews AI shortlists? How can a candidate request a human to look at their application?

6. Check your data practices. Do you have a legal basis for any special category data entering an AI system?

7. Start keeping logs. Record how and when you use high-risk AI. This log can be audited.

None of this is impossible. It's just process.

Which of these 7 steps is furthest from where your agency is today?

posts.blog_title: EU AI Act: What Every Recruiting Agency Must Know About AI Compliance
posts.text:
A recruiter told me last week: "We just use tools — we don't build AI. So the AI Act doesn't really apply to us."

I hear this constantly.

And it's the most dangerous assumption a recruiting agency can make right now.

Imagine this: Your ATS has a built-in scoring feature that ranks candidates before a recruiter sees them. You've used it for two years. It's fast, it works, you barely think about it.

Under the EU AI Act, that scoring feature is classified as high-risk AI. And as the organisation deploying it, you are legally responsible for how it's used — not the vendor that built it.

That means candidates have the right to know it's being used on them. That means a human must be able to override its outputs. That means you need a process candidates can use to request a human review.

Agencies that treat this as "someone else's compliance problem" are going to face a rude awakening in 2026.

The ones that get ahead of it now — by being transparent with candidates, documenting their processes, and designing AI into their workflow responsibly — will actually turn this into a competitive edge.

Clients are already asking about AI governance in supplier audits. Candidates are starting to ask too.

Are you prepared to answer?
